channel.title: Plain Security
channel.description: Two-minute security briefings for the board: how it breaks, what stops it, one suggested first step. The sound of the briefing videos on plain-security.fyi.
channel.itunes:author: Plain Security

item.title: Email security: four ways it breaks
item.description: Interception, tampering, spoofing and man-in-the-middle. What each costs, what stops it.

item.title: Cookie hijacking: how attackers use borrowed credentials
item.description: How stolen or intercepted cookies enable account takeover, bypass MFA, and impersonate users on trusted downstream systems.

item.title: SSL and TLS cipher suites: a layer deeper into encryption in transit
item.description: A layer deeper into encryption in transit: weak suites, downgrades and key exchange. What to ask of IT.

item.title: Ransomware: four steps to a standstill
item.description: One stolen login, four steps to a standstill. What happens at each step, what breaks the chain.

item.title: Decrease the blast radius: the difference between an incident and a crisis
item.description: One breach becomes a total outage — unless networks are segmented, admin is tiered, and permissions are minimal. The difference between an incident and a crisis.

item.title: Phishing: four ways a person gets played
item.description: Fake login pages, MFA fatigue, CEO fraud and every other channel. What one click can and cannot do.

item.title: Passwords and identity: who can get in, and who can do anything
item.description: Reused passwords, phone-read codes, leavers and standing admins. Who can get in, who can do anything.

item.title: Entra ID: the keys to Microsoft 365
item.description: Global Admins, an open Conditional Access gate, guests who never left, and the hybrid sync back door.

item.title: IAM: who may do what, and who checks
item.description: Orphaned service accounts, wildcard roles, one person with both signatures, shared admin logins. With examples.

item.title: Supply chain attacks: breached through someone we trust
item.description: Breached through someone we trust: vendor updates, supplier logins, open-source code and SaaS leaks.

item.title: Cloud misconfiguration: the cloud is secure, our settings are not
item.description: The cloud is secure, our settings are not. Four mistakes behind most cloud breaches, and what prevents each.

item.title: Shared responsibility: whose job is it?
item.description: The provider secures the cloud, you secure what you put in it. Where the line sits for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

item.title: The 90-page report: what a clean opinion does and does not tell you
item.description: Your supplier sent a 90-page assurance report. Which type it is, what period and scope it covers, the controls it assumes you run, how to read the exceptions, and what a clean opinion never tells you.

item.title: Insider threat: four people who already have the keys
item.description: Four people who already have the keys: leaver, careless colleague, unwatched admin, pressured employee.

item.title: DDoS: offline without a break-in
item.description: Offline without a break-in. Floods, fake shoppers, one DNS provider, extortion, what keeps us up.

item.title: Things that expire: domains, DNS and certificates
item.description: Could we go offline because somebody forgot to renew something? Domains, DNS and certificates all carry a date, and public certificates shrink to 47 days by 2029.

item.title: The unpatched server: known hole, published fix, still open
item.description: Known hole, published fix, still open. Four ways patching fails, and the one control that closes each.

item.title: Fixing vulnerabilities with AI: faster, not on autopilot
item.description: How automated and AI vulnerability remediation actually works: ranking, bots and AI that write the fix, auto-merge and poisoned updates, and fixing agents with too much access.

item.title: The box at the edge: who owns it, and is it patched?
item.description: VPN and firewall appliances are the most common way in. Who owns the box, is it patched, is the admin page on the internet, and what zero trust changes.

item.title: php2shell: one request, and the web server is theirs
item.description: Two critical PHP flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) can let anyone run code on a web server without logging in. Update, find old PHP, and ask your suppliers.

item.title: The trusted app that let them in: ConnectWise Cloud Backup
item.description: Attackers stole the keys of a trusted Microsoft 365 backup app and signed in as the app, with no user and no MFA, helped by AI agents. What it means for you, and the questions worth asking.

item.title: Could we restore? Backups, and the restore nobody tested
item.description: If ransomware hits tonight, how long until we are back? Recovery targets in plain words, the copy an attacker cannot delete, the restore nobody tested, and the cloud data nobody backs up.

item.title: Shadow IT: the data you don't know you have
item.description: Company data in tools nobody approved, accounts nobody manages, apps nobody revoked. How to see it again.

item.title: AI at work: four ways it turns on us
item.description: Public chatbots, hijacked assistants, cloned voices and confident nonsense. What each costs, what contains it.

item.title: A sandbox for AI: where should an agent be allowed to run?
item.description: Where should an AI agent be allowed to run? A throwaway machine with its own kernel, no standing keys, a closed door to the internet, and a person at every exit.

item.title: How AI agents work: the model, the harness, and what you plug in
item.description: How AI agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Hermes Agent work: the model and the harness, agents, skills and MCP servers, why to review skills and servers before installing, and what keeps them contained.

item.title: Sovereign cloud: sovereign from whom?
item.description: Sovereign from whom? The EU's own yardstick, the law that follows the provider, what still leaves with your SaaS, and whether you could leave.

item.title: CADA or the framework? Same ladder, different rules
item.description: The Commission's SEAL ladder and the proposed law's four assurance levels. What each is, how the levels work, who would have to comply, three examples.

item.title: Encrypted at rest: who can still read it?
item.description: Encrypted, so safe? Only against a stolen disk. Logins, keys, forgotten copies, and what quantum really changes.

item.title: Quantum and AI: when two threats converge
item.description: Encrypted today, decrypted tomorrow. How quantum computers and AI together threaten current encryption, and why migration must start now.

item.title: Your website is a front door
item.description: Injection, forgotten plugins, account takeover and skimmed checkouts. Four ways in, one control each.

item.title: Endpoints: laptops, phones and the kitchen table
item.description: Lost laptops, unmanaged phones, admin for everyone, an outdated browser. Where the data really lives.

item.title: Knowing what to protect: four ways we lose track of data
item.description: Crown jewels nobody can name, forty copies, links for anyone, data kept fifteen years. How to see it again.

item.title: Would we even notice? Four ways an attack stays invisible
item.description: Logs nobody kept, alerts nobody read, half the estate unwatched, tickets read Monday. Would we notice?

item.title: The factory, the building and the cameras: four ways they stop
item.description: Production lines, building systems and cameras that cannot be patched. Four ways they stop, one fix each.

item.title: Building software that holds
item.description: Secrets in code, a hijacked build server, testing after launch, apps nobody owns. What closes each gap.

item.title: Code security: what is inside the software we ship
item.description: Your own code, open-source parts, server templates and container images: where security flaws hide, and how to tell which ones matter.

item.title: The pentest came back fine. Are we safe now?
item.description: The pentest came back fine. Are we safe now? What was tested and when, how much the tester knew, findings that never get fixed, and the difference between a scan, a pentest and a red team.

item.title: How much security is enough?
item.description: What should we spend, who should the CISO report to, and which numbers should the board see every quarter? Budget benchmarks, the CISO's independence, five numbers for the dashboard, external review, and what NIS2 and DORA ask of the board.

item.title: Buying a company, buying its breaches
item.description: When you buy a company, you also buy its network, its accounts, its data and whoever is already inside. An inherited attacker, the estate nobody listed, connecting on day one, warranties and insurance, and the personal data that comes with the deal.

item.title: Terraform state: the map of everything you run
item.description: What Terraform state is, why it holds the map of your infrastructure and often its passwords, locking and versions, the chicken-and-egg of where it lives, and HCP Terraform, GitLab, S3 and Azure compared.

item.title: We sell products with software in them. What does the CRA ask of us, and from when?
item.description: We sell products with software in them. What the CRA asks of makers, importers and resellers: reporting since September 2026, CE mark and support period from December 2027.

item.title: The first 72 hours. Four ways they go wrong.
item.description: Who decides, what gets wiped, who says what, who to call. How the first three days derail.

item.title: Cyber insurance: four surprises at claim time
item.description: The policy is a control with small print. Questionnaire, exclusions, sub-limits, notification: what each costs.

item.title: NIS2 and DORA: the law now names the board
item.description: The law now names the board. Four things that changed, and what has to be in place before the audit.

item.title: Cbw and Wwke: one date, two kinds of resilience
item.description: Two Dutch laws started on 15 August 2026: one for cyber, one for physical resilience. Which one applies to you, what differs, and the one board decision that covers both.

item.title: You are the target: four routes in
item.description: Board members are a route in: private mail and phones, a cloned voice on a call, the board pack, and travel. Four routes, and what closes each.

item.title: Eight ways to prove who you are
item.description: OAuth2, SAML, OIDC, mTLS, passkeys, Kerberos, LDAP, RADIUS, API keys and AI agents. When to use each, where it breaks, and what AI changes.
